source.title: Transformer-based Cross-Modal Recipe Embeddings with Large Batch Training
source.authors: Jing Yang; Jun-Wen Chen; Keiji Yanai

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper; no material problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on held-out retrieval performance in cross-modal recipe embedding, a new setting relative to V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-set retrieval and image-generation metrics across batch sizes. Retrieval rows bear on held-out performance; image-generation FID does not measure the behavior named in a claim version. Cited results from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The batch-size experiments measure cross-modal recipe retrieval and conditional image generation, rather than the image-classification or language-model performance specified by V5. They test a related claim outside the supplied versions. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that larger batches benefit recipe retrieval up to diminishing returns, with a small decline at 1024, while worsening conditional image-generation performance in the reported sweep; they describe this as a trade-off.
record.recipe_differences: Cross-modal retrieval on Recipe1M, with Transformer encoders and Adam; reports retrieval and generation metrics rather than training/test error gaps. The batch-size sweep's epoch budget is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes retrieval and image-generation metrics; image encoder backbone (ViT-B versus CLIP-ViT) also changes retrieval performance.

fits_no_version.finding: On Recipe1M retrieval, increasing batch size from 64 to 768 improves TNLBT-V R@1 from 36.6 to 48.0 and TNLBT-C R@1 from 48.0 to 56.5. At 1024, these decline slightly to 47.5 and 56.0. Median rank does not capture the latter declines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger training batches can improve held-out cross-modal contrastive retrieval, with diminishing benefits and small declines at sufficiently large sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5 reports worsening generation FID from batch 64 to 768: 17.9 to 46.4 for TNLBT-V and 16.5 to 69.7 for TNLBT-C.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing batch size can worsen conditional image-generation quality while improving retrieval in a joint embedding framework.

record.problems: No training-error measurements or train/test gap; batch-sweep epoch budget is not stated; the reported outcome is retrieval performance, not error rate. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Image-generation FID results across batch sizes in Table 5 were left out because they do not measure held-out retrieval or the training/test generalization gap named by the versions.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and comparison with natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width-dependent test error beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size penalties and remedies for image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Section 4.1 supplies general training schedules of 50 epochs for TNLBT-V and 20 frozen plus 100 unfrozen epochs for TNLBT-C; Section 4.5 does not explicitly confirm their application to every batch condition. Missing training-error measurements would not alone disqualify a held-out-performance test of V5. The decisive mismatch here is the task and outcome specified by the version. The linked GitHub repository implements FID and is not evidence that the study released its own training code.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.

Image-classification and language-model error or performance; explicit training-versus-test gap; whether epoch budgets were held fixed in the batch-size sweep; recipe adaptations such as warmup or normalization changes.
Sharpness or other trained-network properties as predictors of generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
